content: The term incertae sedis, which translates to of uncertain position (seat), is used in taxonomy to describe a group whose broader relationships within the biological classification system are either unknown or undefined. For example, the taxonomy of humans is typically recognized as follows: Empire Neomura: Includes all living organisms. Domain Eukaryota: Includes all nucleated organisms. Kingdom Animalia: Includes all animals. Phylum Chordata: Includes all vertebrates and invertebrate chordates. Class Mammalia: Includes all mammals. Order Primates: Includes all primates. Family Hominidae: Includes all apes. Subfamily Homininae: Includes gorillas and chimpanzees. Tribe Hominini: Includes chimpanzees. Subtribe Hominina: Includes Australopithecus and prehistoric humans. Genus Homo: Includes Homo erectus and other prehistoric humans. Species Homo sapiens: Refers to modern humans. If modern humans were newly discovered or considered a taxonomic enigma, they might be assigned the rank of incertae sedis. For instance, if the relationship of the genus Homo to other members of the family Hominidae were unclear, a list of great apes might appear as follows: Kingdom Animalia Phylum Chordata Class Mammalia Order Primates Family Hominidae Genus Homo (incertae sedis) Subfamily Ponginae: Includes orangutans. Subfamily Homininae: Includes gorillas and chimpanzees. Similarly, if humans were known to be primates but their other relationships were unclear, a taxonomy of primates might look like this: Kingdom Animalia Phylum Chordata Class Mammalia Order Primates Genus Homo (incertae sedis) Family Cercopithecidae: Includes Old World monkeys. Family Hominidae: Includes apes. Family Lemuridae: Includes lemurs. Reasons a group might be considered incertae sedis: 1. Not included in an analysis: If a formal phylogenetic analysis does not include a specific taxon, researchers may label it incertae sedis rather than speculating about its placement. This is common in molecular phylogenies, as obtaining tissue samples from rare organisms can be challenging. It is also frequent with fossil taxa, as many fossils are defined based on incomplete information. For example, if a phylogeny is constructed using soft tissue and vertebrae as primary characters, but a taxon is only known from a single tooth, it would be necessary to label it incertae sedis. 2. Controversy: If conflicting results exist or there is no consensus among researchers about how a taxon relates to other organisms, it may be listed as incertae sedis until the conflict is resolved. 3. Basal taxa: There is a growing trend in phylogenetic taxonomy to place basal taxa within the clade containing their ancestors but to refrain from assigning them more specific taxonomic ranks. For example, the ancestor of all primates would be placed in the order Primates but not assigned to a specific family. Assigning it to a family, such as Lemuridae, would imply a closer relationship to lemurs than to other primates, which may not be accurate, as it is equally related to all primates.
